title: Neral's Unexpected Adventure
markdown:
Wizard Neral had finally acquired a brand-new quill, the kind that whispered secrets onto parchment, with a tip so fine it could tickle a dewdrop. He spent ages arranging his mandrake roots just so, humming softly. Imagine a land so high the air tasted like frozen honey, and the only sound was the lonely echo of mule bells between sheer rocky ridges. Moonlight, thick as clotted cream, would gather on the snowdrifts. This was Neral’s domain, and he cherished quiet days above all else.

“Ah, Pipkin,” he sighed to his jackdaw companion, perched like a feathered shadow on his shoulder, glossy black feathers catching the lamplight, “today we do nothing. Absolutely, gloriously, nothing. Not a single incantation, not a single potion. Just peace.”

Pipkin, a jackdaw of discerning taste, simply ruffled his wings. He had been chosen by Neral not for prestige, or because he could magically levitate teacups, but because he noticed things. Like the faint scent of lavender Neral always wore, or the way his eyebrow twitched when he was thinking very hard about the best way to arrange his mandrake roots. Pipkin was Neral’s silent partner in observing the world, and he often offered his own unique brand of encouragement with a knowing clack of his beak.

But peace, as Neral knew from countless slightly-less-quiet days, was a slippery thing. It had a habit of scampering off like a startled mountain hare. The very instant Neral dipped his new quill, eager to sketch the perfect cloud formation, a creature of impressive size arrived, making the teacups on a nearby shelf rattle. It was Marmalade, Neral’s familiar, a ginger cat of magnificent girth and an expression that could curdle milk faster than any spoiled potion. She sat directly on his open spellbook, tail twitching imperiously, a furry orange comma of disapproval.

“Meow,” Marmalade announced, a sound that vibrated with pure feline authority. Neral understood her perfectly. It meant: Right. You’re hired. Let’s get on with it. And that quill looks dreadfully boring.

Neral blinked, carefully prepared spell components momentarily forgotten. “Hired? Marmalade, my dear, I believe you’ll find it’s the other way around. I hire you to be a cat, mostly. And not to shed on my scrolls, which you seem to be doing right now.”

Marmalade narrowed her emerald eyes, twin chips of ancient jade. “Mrow,” she stated firmly, a low rumble in her chest that Neral recognised as absolute seriousness. This translated to: Nonsense. I have a pressing engagement that requires your immediate attention. I require the Sparkle-Stone. Before sundown. And if you fail, consider our arrangement terminated. Immediately. Which would be terribly inconvenient for you.

Neral, a wizard who prided himself on meticulous preparation and scheduled relaxation, felt a tremor of panic. A terminated arrangement with Marmalade was a truly dire prospect. It meant more unsolicited naps on his head during important spellcasting, and an alarming tendency for her to bat at his beard with surprising force. “The Sparkle-Stone? Where on earth is it?” he asked, already reaching for his worn travelling cloak.

“The Whispering Peaks,” Marmalade declared, stretching languidly. She hopped off the spellbook, leaving a faint ginger smudge that Neral knew would take a special cleaning charm to remove. “Do try not to dawdle. My time is valuable, and frankly, the sun is setting on my patience.”

And so Neral’s quiet day evaporated like mist in the morning sun. He grabbed his knapsack, stuffing it with emergency biscuits, a flask of lukewarm chamomile tea, and a small anti-procrastination charm that hummed faintly. “Right then, Pipkin,” he said, voice a little too cheerful. “An unexpected excursion. Always good for the constitution, wouldn’t you agree? Builds character.”

Pipkin gave a knowing clack of his beak. He’d seen this before. Neral loved planning not to do things, and when those plans were so rudely interrupted, he always rallied with a misplaced enthusiasm. Pipkin, however, was already mentally reviewing the best routes through the foothills.

They set off towards the Whispering Peaks, the air growing thinner and the wind gaining a playful mischievous bite. It swirled around them, tugging at Neral’s cloak and ruffling Pipkin’s feathers. Neral, ever the planner, had packed a perfectly balanced picnic, designed for maximum sustenance and minimal fuss. He imagined a delightful uneventful feast amidst breathtaking scenery. Mountain winds, however, are absolute hooligans when it comes to airborne pastries. A sudden boisterous gust, strong enough to make the very pines sway like drunken dancers and whip Neral’s beard into a frenzy, snatched his knapsack right out of his hands. Biscuits, cheese, a perfectly crisp apple: all tumbled and spiralled into the vast rocky expanse below, becoming a feast for the mountain goats.

“Oh, botheration,” Neral yelped, watching his carefully curated meal disappear. “My emergency provisions. That was precisely the cheese I had aged for six months.”

Pipkin peered over the edge, then chirped a sound that was suspiciously like a chuckle. No food. Stakes just doubled. Now they were not just on an errand; they were on a hungry errand.

They trudged onward, hunger gnawing at Neral’s stomach with an almost feline intensity. The path narrowed, becoming a precarious ledge that skirted a dizzying drop, the sheer rock face disappearing into mist below. The wind moaned like a lonely spirit, carrying the faint distant cry of a hawk, and the chill bit at his exposed cheeks. It was here, with the wind whipping around him and his stomach rumbling a mournful tune, that Neral had a realisation. His carefully laid plans for a day of quiet contemplation were now in tatters. He had promised himself he would rest. But rest, he was learning, did not always mean doing nothing. Sometimes it meant finding a new way to achieve peace, even amidst chaos. He looked at Pipkin, who was watching him with those bright intelligent eyes.

“Pipkin,” Neral said, voice suddenly firm, shedding the last vestiges of his hunger-induced gloom. “My eyes aren’t what they used to be for spotting tiny stones, especially when there’s wind trying to steal my spectacles. Yours, however…”

Pipkin puffed out his chest, a proud iridescent shimmer. He had the best eyes on the eastern slope, capable of spotting a single lost berry from a mile away. Neral decided to trust his companion’s keen vision, a departure from his usual reliance on scrolls and charts.

Just as they rounded a jagged outcrop, a fearsome grumble echoed through the pass, a sound like rocks tumbling downhill. Blocking their way was Gruff, a troll whose skin looked like rough granite, encrusted with lichens, and whose beard was a tangled mossy mess that smelled faintly of damp earth. He brandished a club that looked suspiciously like a fallen pine tree, still sporting a few stubborn branches.

“Halt,” Gruff boomed. “No one passes without paying the troll toll. Shiny things. Give Gruff shiny things. Or Gruff gets very cross.”

Behind them, Neral heard a faint insistent mrow. Marmalade, having evidently decided her time was too valuable to wait by the hearth, had followed, tail leading the way. The pressure was building, a two-headed monster of demands, and Neral’s carefully calibrated anti-procrastination charm felt about as useful as a chocolate teapot.

Neral, caught between a hungry troll and an impatient cat, took a deep breath. His mind, usually a library of intricate spells, felt a bit like a dishevelled bookshelf. “Gruff, my good fellow,” he began, trying to sound more in command than he felt. “I have no shiny things, alas. My knapsack, you see, was waylaid by a rather enthusiastic gust of wind. But I do have a story. And a very useful stone.” He held up a smooth grey river stone he’d picked up earlier, its coolness a small comfort in his palm. “This stone is the Stone of Untold Tales. It hums with the whispers of the world. Listen closely.”

Gruff squinted, small piggy eyes narrowed. He wasn’t much for tales; he had always preferred a good rumble. But he was intrigued by the idea of humming stones. Pipkin, sensing the shift, swooped down with a loud caw, darting past Gruff’s nose like a black arrow, a tiny whirlwind of feathers and noise.

“And my companion,” Neral continued, grabbing the opportunity, “is a creature of the air. He can find anything, but only if his master is sufficiently well-provisioned. And perhaps well-accompanied.” He gave Gruff a meaningful look, then winked at Pipkin, who was now perching precariously on the troll’s knobbly shoulder, looking for all the world like an accidental decoration.

Gruff, quite proud of his own knobbiness and now thoroughly distracted by Pipkin’s antics, leaned closer to the jackdaw. “Untold tales, you say? And this bird… he finds things? Important things?”

“Precisely,” Neral said, pushing the ordinary stone towards Gruff with a flourish. “He can find you the most peculiar magnificent things. Take this stone. It’s rather potent. Full of secrets.”

Gruff, captivated by Pipkin’s aerial acrobatics and the idea of potent secret-filled stones, grumbled. He liked things that hummed, and he rather liked the idea of a bird that could find him more of them. He took the river stone, turning it over in his enormous calloused hand. Pipkin, with a final conspiratorial clack, hopped back to Neral’s shoulder.

And there, nestled in a crevice Gruff had been guarding, glinting even in the dim light with an almost defiant sparkle, was a stone that shimmered with every colour imaginable. It pulsed with a soft internal light, like a captured sunrise. The Sparkle-Stone.

“Remarkable,” Neral breathed. He’d done it. Not with grand spells or heroic feats of strength, but with a bit of quick thinking, a dash of theatrical flair, and a very understanding jackdaw who knew exactly when to create a diversion.

They hurried back, Pipkin’s happy chirps filling the air. The moonlight was painting the snow-covered peaks in shades of silver and lavender. As they descended, they passed a waterfall, its cascading water catching the moon, turning it into a sheet of liquid silver tumbling silently into the valley below. Neral knew he would remember it far more vividly than any meticulously drawn sketch.

Back at their cosy cottage, the fire crackled merrily. Marmalade sat by the hearth, the Sparkle-Stone nestled in her paws, purring with deep satisfaction. She did not say thank you. That was not her style, and Neral did not expect it. The rumbling in her chest was more eloquent than any words. Neral, sharing a crust of bread saved from his own emergency stash, looked at his familiar and his feathered friend.

“Well, Pipkin,” Neral said with a fond smile, stroking Marmalade’s warm flank. “It seems my quiet day turned into quite the adventure after all.” Pipkin nodded sagely. The new quill remained untouched. The Sparkle-Stone, however, was exactly where a cat had intended it to be, which was, for Neral, a kind of peace he had not scheduled.
characters: Neral (a quiet-day wizard), Pipkin (a discerning jackdaw)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
